title: Linear Equations and Inequalities in One Variable
lead: Your first Math class. These questions are the backbone of the Algebra domain. They show up as “what is the value of x?”, “what is the value of this expression?”, “how many solutions does the equation have?”, and as word problems. Most students already know how to solve these. The points are lost to careless slips, so the habit this class builds is writing every step down.

parts.title: Part 1 · The core idea
parts.html:
A linear equation is built from numbers and a variable raised only to the first power: no x², no √x, no 1/x. With an equals sign it is an equation, such as 3x + 4 = 19. With >, <, ≥ or ≤ it is an inequality, such as 3x + 4 > 19.

Solving means getting the variable alone on one side and a number on the other. One rule keeps the equation true the whole way: whatever you do to one side, do exactly the same to the other.

3x+4=19 Subtract 4 from both sides → 3x=15
Divide both sides by 3 → x=5

parts.title: Part 2 · Combining like terms and distributing
parts.html:
Like terms. Terms with the same variable add like ordinary numbers: 4x + 2x = 6x, and 7x − x = 6x. When x appears on both sides, move every x term to one side and every number to the other.

5x−7=11−x Add 7 to both sides → 5x=18−x
Add x to both sides → 6x=18
Divide both sides by 6 → x=3

Distributing. A number in front of parentheses multiplies every term inside: 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6. Students most often forget the second term.

3(x+2)=11 Distribute → 3x+6=11
Subtract 6 from both sides → 3x=5
Divide both sides by 3 → x=53

An answer that is a fraction is normal on the SAT. Do not assume you made a mistake because the answer is not a whole number.

Common mistake. Sign errors when a term changes sides. 5x + 3 = 2x + 11 becomes 5x − 2x = 11 − 3, not 11 + 3. Write the intermediate line instead of doing it in your head.

parts.title: Part 3 · Fractions and negative numbers
parts.html:
Fractions and negatives do not change the method. They only make slips more likely. Two rules of thumb for fractions:

  • Only the coefficient of x is a fraction: leave it until the last step, then multiply by its reciprocal.
  • Several fractions: clear them all in the first step by multiplying both sides by a common multiple of the denominators.
(23)x+1=7 Subtract 1 from both sides → (23)x=6
Multiply both sides by 32 → x=9
x3+5=x2−1 Multiply every term by 6 → 2x+30=3x−6
Subtract 2x from both sides → 30=x−6
Add 6 to both sides → x=36
Check: 363+5=17 and 362−1=17

The check takes 10 seconds and catches almost every sign error.

Negative numbers. A negative times a negative is positive; a positive times a negative is negative. The place this matters most is distributing a negative number.

−3(x−4)=5 Distribute: −3 times −4 is +12 → −3x+12=5
Subtract 12 from both sides → −3x=−7
Divide both sides by −3 → x=73

parts.title: Part 4 · Two question types to recognize
parts.html:
Two variables, one value given. If an equation has x and y and the question tells you one of them, substitute it and solve for the other.

If 3x+4y=2 and x=−2, what is the value of y? Substitute → 3(−2)+4y=2 → −6+4y=2
Add 6 to both sides → 4y=8
Divide both sides by 4 → y=2

“What is the value of this expression?” The question gives an equation and asks for a different expression, not for x. There are two ways to answer:

  1. Solve for x, then substitute it into the expression.
  2. Look for a relationship between the equation and the expression, and skip solving.
If 3x+2=11, what is the value of 12x+8? Way 1: 3x=9, so x=3, and 12(3)+8=44
Way 2: 12x+8=4(3x+2)=4(11)=44

The first way always works. The second is faster when you can see it, and it matters most when x would come out as an awkward fraction. Before you finish, reread what was asked: giving x when the question wanted the expression is a common way to lose the point.

parts.title: Part 5 · Inequalities
parts.html:
An inequality is solved with the same steps as an equation. The one thing to watch is the direction of the sign, and it depends on the coefficient of x.

Positive coefficient: the sign stays.

3x+4>19 Subtract 4 from both sides → 3x>15
Divide both sides by 3 → x>5

Every number greater than 5 works, and 5 itself and anything below it does not. You can confirm by testing one value on each side: x = 6 gives 22 > 19, which is true; x = 4 gives 16 > 19, which is false.

Negative coefficient: the sign reverses. When you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, > becomes < and ≥ becomes ≤.

−3x+4>19 Subtract 4 from both sides → −3x>15
Divide both sides by −3 and reverse the sign → x<−5

Test it: x = −6 gives 18 + 4 = 22 > 19, true. x = 0 gives 4 > 19, false. Forgetting to reverse the sign is the most common error in this topic, and testing one value takes a few seconds and catches it.

The SAT sometimes asks which value is a solution. Solve the inequality first, then check each choice against it. Class 18 covers inequalities in full, including graphs and systems.

parts.title: Part 6 · One, none, or infinitely many solutions
parts.html:
Most linear equations have exactly one solution. The other two cases only happen when the equation is built for it, so these questions usually contain a constant such as a and ask what value produces each case. Simplify the equation and see what is left:

What is leftSolutionsWhy
x = a numberOneOnly that value works.
A false statement, such as 6 = 10NoneThe x terms cancelled and the numbers disagree. No value of x can fix that.
A true statement, such as 6 = 6Infinitely manyBoth sides were the same expression, so every value of x works.
3x−2=ax−5. If a=3, how many solutions does the equation have? Substitute a=3 → 3x−2=3x−5
Subtract 3x from both sides → −2=−5
False for every x → no solution
3x−6=a(x−2). For what value of a does the equation have infinitely many solutions? Distribute → 3x−6=ax−2a
The sides are identical when a=3: 3x−6=3x−6
For any other a there is one solution, x=2

The shortcut: compare the two sides once they are simplified. Same x coefficient and different constants means no solution. Same x coefficient and same constants means infinitely many. Different x coefficients means exactly one.

parts.title: Part 7 · Word problems
parts.html:
Word problems here are translation exercises. Learn the dictionary:

WordsMeaning
is=
more than, sumadd
less thansubtract, in the order said: “5 less than x” is x − 5, not 5 − x
perdivide or multiply, depending on the setup
at least≥
at most≤

Two traps. “Less than” flips the order, and it is the most-tested translation trap. And some questions ask for an expression, not a solution: after translating, stop. Do not solve something that is not asked.

parts.title: Part 8 · The Desmos shortcut
parts.html:
For a “what is the value of x” question, type the left side into Desmos as one expression and the right side as another. Desmos draws two lines and puts a dot where they cross. Click the dot: its x-coordinate is the answer. Ten seconds, no sign errors.

Use algebra for “how many solutions” questions, since they ask about the structure of the equation. Desmos is the visual check there: parallel lines mean no solution, identical lines mean infinitely many.

parts.title: Part 9 · Things to remember
parts.html:
• Equations: whatever you do to one side, do to the other. Write every step.
  • Inequalities: the sign keeps its direction when you divide by a positive number and reverses when you divide by a negative number.
  • Number of solutions: x = a number means one; a false statement means none; a true statement means infinitely many.
  • Before you answer: check whether the question asks for x or for an expression.

parts.title: Part 10 · Harder moves with equations
parts.html:
Solve for what is asked, not always for x. Before isolating a variable, look at what the question wants. If it asks for an expression, there is often a one-step route.

If 4x + 12y = 20, what is the value of x + 3y? Divide both sides by 4 → x+3y=5
There is no need to find x or y, and with one equation you could not.
If 5(2x − 1) + 3 = 38, what is the value of 2x − 1? Treat 2x−1 as one block
5(2x−1)=35 → 2x−1=7

Isolating a variable that appears twice. Collect every term that contains it on one side, then factor it out.

Solve p = q / (2q + r) for q. Multiply by the denominator → p(2q+r)=q
Expand → 2pq+pr=q
Collect the q terms → pr=q−2pq
Factor → pr=q(1−2p)
Divide → q=pr1−2p

A square root gives two answers when you take it yourself. If x² = 25, then x = 5 or −5. But the symbol √25 means only 5. The ± belongs to the step of solving, not to the root sign.

What is the sum of the solutions of (x − 4)² = 49? x−4=7 or x−4=−7
x=11 or x=−3 → sum 8

Dividing by an expression can lose a solution.

(x + 2)(x − 7) = 3(x + 2) Tempting: divide both sides by (x+2) → x−7=3 → x=10
That step assumes x+2 is not zero, and x=−2 makes both sides 0, so it is a solution too.
Safe: move everything to one side and factor → (x+2)(x−10)=0 → x=−2 or x=10

The opposite problem, a false solution that appears after multiplying or squaring, is covered with rational equations in Class 21 and radical equations in Class 12. The rule for both: dividing can lose solutions, multiplying or squaring can add them, so check your results in the original equation.
